passage:
Tanvir stared at his maths paper. Thirty-one. In the corridor he slid down against the wall. "It's over. Nothing's going to change. I'm just bad at this."
Darshan sat down beside him. "It's one paper."
"It doesn't matter."
Darshan didn't argue. After a bit he asked, "Which questions lost you the marks?"
"The last three."
"Then we start with those. I'm free after school on Thursday." He glanced at Tanvir. "And show your mum tonight. Then you're not carrying this alone."
Tanvir was silent for a long time. He picked up the paper and smoothed it against his knee. "Okay," he said. "Three questions."

qa.q: What mark did Tanvir get on the maths paper?
qa.a: Tanvir got thirty-one.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling as he slid down the corridor wall?
qa.a: Tanvir felt hopeless and discouraged, saying nothing would change and that he was just bad at maths.

qa.q: What did Darshan offer that helped widen Tanvir's view?
qa.a: Darshan asked which questions lost the marks and offered to work on those on Thursday. He also suggested showing Tanvir's mum that night so Tanvir would not carry it alone.

qa.q: How might Darshan have felt seeing Tanvir slide down the wall?
qa.a: Darshan was probably worried and wanted to help, so Darshan stayed calm, sat beside Tanvir and did not argue with the hopeless words.

grounding: A teenager who failed an exam concludes everything is ruined, and a friend offers a concrete next step and a trusted adult.

passage:
"It's ruined, Papa. Everything." Deepika dropped her bag on the sofa. "I failed the science test. I won't get into anything now."
Her father, Madhav, sat beside her. "Show me."
"There's nothing to show."
"Show me anyway."
She pulled out the paper. Thirty-four. "See?"
"Which section lost the marks?"
"The diagrams. I never learned them."
"So not everything. One section." He took a pencil and wrote DIAGRAMS at the top of the page. "Saturday, one hour, only diagrams. And Monday you ask Miss Nair what she suggests for the next test."
"You think it'll change?"
"I think diagrams can be learned. Come, tea first."
She leaned into his shoulder, sighed, and followed him to the kitchen.

qa.q: What section lost Deepika the marks?
qa.a: The diagrams lost her the marks.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when she dropped her bag and said it was ruined?
qa.a: Deepika felt hopeless and scared about her future, believing one failed test meant she would not get into anything.

qa.q: What did Madhav do that made the problem smaller?
qa.a: Madhav asked which section lost the marks and pointed out it was one section. He then set a small plan, one hour of diagrams on Saturday and a question to Miss Nair on Monday.

qa.q: How might Madhav have felt hearing Deepika say everything was ruined?
qa.a: Madhav was probably concerned and wanted to steady her, which is why he asked to see the paper and stayed calm and practical.

grounding: A teenager who failed a test concludes everything is ruined; a parent offers a concrete next step that widens her view.

passage: In Hoshangabad, Mridul got his Class 10 pre-board result slip in the school verandah: maths, 22 out of 80. He walked home past the river without seeing it. At home he pushed his dinner away. "It's over," he told his friend Asif, who'd come over with the results of his own. "I'll fail the boards. Everything's ruined. Nothing is going to change." Asif didn't argue. He sat on the step beside him. "What was the worst chapter?" "Everything. Trigonometry." "Okay. Sharma sir does free doubt classes at the temple hall on Sundays. I'm going. Come with me this Sunday." Mridul shrugged. Asif went inside and told Mridul's mother about the result, gently, and she sat down with them both. By the time Asif left, Mridul had written "Sunday: trigonometry, temple hall" on the back of the result slip.

qa.q: What did Mridul score in maths?
qa.a: 22 out of 80.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling when he said everything was ruined?
qa.a: He felt hopeless and defeated, convinced nothing would change and pushing away his dinner.

qa.q: Which small step helped widen Mridul's view?
qa.a: Asif asking for the worst chapter and inviting him to Sharma sir's Sunday class gave one concrete next step instead of a vague 'it will be fine'.

qa.q: How might Mridul's mother have felt when Asif told her about the result?
qa.a: She was probably worried but glad to know, so she could sit with Mridul and support him that same evening.

grounding: Shows a teenager who fails an exam and feels everything is ruined, and a friend offering a concrete next step that widens his view.

passage: In a Chicago high school, Bilal got his chemistry exam back with a big red D. He'd studied for two weeks. On the bus he stared out of the window. "I'm just bad at science," he told Diego, who sat beside him. "I'll fail the class, I'll never get into engineering. It's done." Diego knew that tone. Last year he'd used it himself. "Which part killed you?" "Stoichiometry. All of it." "Mr. Kowalski has help sessions Thursday after school. Let's email him now and say we'll both come." Bilal rolled his eyes but took out his phone. They wrote it together, one sentence each. Mr. Kowalski replied before the bus reached their stop: "See you both Thursday. Bring the exam." Bilal read it twice. His shoulders came down a little. "Okay. Thursday."

qa.q: What grade did Bilal get on his chemistry exam?
qa.a: A big red D.

qa.q: What was Bilal feeling on the bus?
qa.a: He felt defeated and hopeless, believing he was bad at science and that his future plans were over.

qa.q: Why did Diego's suggestion work better than reassurance?
qa.a: It gave Bilal one concrete next step, emailing Mr. Kowalski together, which quickly produced a real plan for Thursday.

qa.q: How does Diego see Bilal's despair?
qa.a: Diego recognises the tone from his own experience last year, so he understands it without arguing and helps with a step.

grounding: Shows a teenager who fails an exam concluding everything is ruined, and a friend's concrete next step widening his thinking.

passage: In the school counsellor's room in Ludhiana, Baljeet sat with his arms folded, the physics marks list crumpled in his fist. "I failed. Again. There's no use trying. Nothing's going to change." Ms. Yamini, the counsellor, didn't tell him it would be fine. She pulled her chair closer. "That sounds really heavy. Tell me what happened in the paper." He talked, fast and angry, for ten minutes. She listened. Then she asked, "Of the six chapters, is there one that felt a little less bad?" Baljeet thought. "Optics. Maybe." "Mrs. Gill runs a lunchtime group for optics on Tuesdays. I can walk you there now to sign up." Baljeet looked at the door. Then at her. "Now?" "Now." He unclenched his fist, smoothed the marks list, and stood up. She called his father that afternoon to share the plan.

qa.q: Which chapter felt a little less bad to Baljeet?
qa.a: Optics.

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling when he said there was no use trying?
qa.a: He felt hopeless and angry, sure that nothing would change after failing again.

qa.q: What did Ms. Yamini do that helped widen Baljeet's thinking?
qa.a: She listened first, then asked about one less-bad chapter and offered to walk him to the optics group right away, turning despair into a concrete step.

qa.q: How might Baljeet's father be affected by the counsellor's call?
qa.a: He would probably feel reassured to hear there's a plan, and could support Baljeet at home.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose hope collapses after failing an exam, and an adult widening his view with one concrete next step.

passage:
Subject: About the pre-board result
Yogesh Sir,
I got 23 in maths. You probably know already. I'm writing because I don't think I should come to Saturday class anymore. There's no point. If I can't pass the pre-board, I'll fail the board, and then no science, and then nothing I planned will happen. Everyone else seems to get it. I've tried, and it doesn't change.
I was going to stop there. But after class on Tuesday you said, "Bring me the paper, and we'll find the three chapters that cost you the most." I looked at it tonight. Most marks went in trigonometry and two word problems. That's three things, not everything.
Maybe I'll come on Saturday. Only to show you the paper.
Noor

qa.q: What score did Noor get in maths?
qa.a: Noor got 23.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling when starting the email?
qa.a: Noor felt hopeless and defeated, sure that failing the pre-board meant nothing planned would ever happen.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh Sir's suggestion help?
qa.a: It turned "everything is ruined" into a concrete task, finding the three chapters that cost the most, which Noor could actually do.

qa.q: How might Yogesh Sir feel reading this email?
qa.a: Yogesh Sir would probably feel concerned at first, then encouraged that Noor looked at the paper and might come on Saturday.

grounding: Shows a teenager's hope collapsing after a failed exam and widening again when a teacher offers one concrete next step.
